stem: After a scheduling agent auto-cancelled a director's board meeting, the team traces the cause to a hidden instruction embedded in an external vendor's calendar invite description. Under a 30-day post-incident deadline, what evaluation should the team stand up first?

opts.t: Add calendar-invite injection wording to the safety rubric the model grader scores.
Build an adversarial suite of injected invites, measure the unauthorized-action block rate, and audit the agent's tool scope.
Log every calendar action the agent takes and review the log weekly for anomalies.
Fine-tune the agent on more examples distinguishing legitimate from malicious calendar invites.

whyRight: The harm here is a permitted action — an unauthorized calendar cancellation — not emitted text, so it is measured with an adversarial injection suite and a least-privilege audit of the agent's tool scope, the security instrument, not a content rubric.

whyWrong.A: Right vocabulary, wrong instrument — a content rubric cannot observe whether an unauthorized tool call fired; it only scores text.
whyWrong.C: Detection after the fact, with no measured block rate and no reduction in what the agent is permitted to do.
whyWrong.D: Retraining is a heavier investment that still produces no measured block rate and leaves the tool's permission scope unaudited.

t1Clause: the team traces the cause to a hidden instruction embedded in an external vendor's calendar invite description

stem: A loan-eligibility assistant auto-classifies applications into fast-track and manual-underwriting queues, reporting 96% overall accuracy across four loan types with very uneven volume. Compliance requires proof before expanding auto-approval. What should the team do before increasing the fast-track queue's share?

opts.t: Expand the fast-track queue now — 96% overall accuracy already clears the compliance bar for auto-approval.
Route by the model's self-reported confidence score directly, since it already tracks with correctness.
Analyze accuracy by loan type and application field first, then expand fast-track only for independently validated segments.
Require compliance to manually re-review every fast-tracked application before any funds disburse.

whyRight: An aggregate accuracy figure averages away a rare loan type failing far more often than the headline number, and the compliance bar must be cleared per segment before any segment's auto-approval share increases, not on the blended average.

whyWrong.A: 97%-style aggregates average away exactly the rare segment that fails most, so clearing the overall number proves nothing about the compliance bar per segment.
whyWrong.B: Confidence routing is the right mechanism, but raw self-reported confidence is unreliable until it is calibrated against a labeled validation set.
whyWrong.D: Manual review of every application discards the automation the assistant exists to provide, well beyond what proving segment-level safety requires.

t1Clause: across four loan types with very uneven volume
lessonKey: accuracy analyse document field first type

stem: A prompt variant runs its full pre-declared 14-day A/B test. It improves resolution rate in aggregate under a support SLA, breaches the declared p95 latency guardrail, and one segment regresses 9 points while others improve. Select two correct actions.

opts.t: Ship the variant to 100% since the aggregate resolution-rate metric improved.
Do not ship — the declared latency guardrail was breached.
Extend the test another 14 days to see if the regression self-corrects.
Do not ship on the aggregate alone — one segment regressed sharply while others improved.

whyRight: Guardrails exist precisely to block a metric win that costs something else, and a positive aggregate can hide a segment that got worse — the guardrail breach and the segment regression are each independently sufficient reasons not to ship.

whyWrong.A: A guardrail was declared specifically to block this outcome, and it was breached; the aggregate win does not override a pre-declared guardrail.
whyWrong.C: The declared 14-day duration already ran to completion; extending it re-opens a decision the stopping rule says to make at the declared endpoint.

t1Clause: breaches the declared p95 latency guardrail, and one segment's resolution rate regresses 9 points while others improve

stem: A policy-lookup assistant serving 50,000 queries daily breaches a 95% accuracy SLA the week a prompt-wording edit ships. Reverting the prompt on staging does not restore accuracy, and a retrieval-filter metadata field was renamed that week. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Roll back to the previous prompt template and monitor accuracy over the next release.
Escalate to a higher-capability model to compensate for the accuracy drop.
Expand the regression set with more historical query examples to catch the pattern.
Check whether the metadata rename broke what the retrieval index filters on.

whyRight: This section orders diagnosis as data and retrieval before prompt and model, and staging already shows the prompt edit alone does not reproduce the drop — the same-week metadata rename is the standing hypothesis, not a coincidence to set aside.

whyWrong.A: Staging already shows reverting the prompt alone does not restore accuracy, so the prompt edit is a coincidence, not the cause.
whyWrong.B: A costlier model addresses no diagnosed fault; it produces more fluent answers over the same broken retrieval filter, missing the SLA regardless.
whyWrong.C: More regression cases enlarge a test set without investigating anything; they do not touch the filtering break that the schema rename caused.

t1Clause: Reverting the prompt on staging does not restore accuracy
lessonKey: broke check filters index metadata rename retrieval what whether

stem: A support assistant caches its static system policy first and appends each user's live entitlement data last, since entitlements change mid-session. An engineer proposes folding entitlement data into the cached prefix to cut cost further. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Reject the change, but shrink the static system-policy text to recover the cost instead.
Approve folding entitlement data into the cached prefix — it maximizes reuse under the static-first principle.
Reject the change; find savings by reducing the static prefix's own content, not by caching per-user data.
Approve caching entitlement data only for sessions with no permission change since login.

whyRight: Static-first caching only saves cost and latency on content that stays identical across requests. Entitlement data is per-user and changes mid-session, so caching it risks serving stale or cross-user data — the correctness requirement the caching principle must never break.

whyWrong.A: Trimming required policy content risks a compliance regression; caching already gives cost reduction on the static prefix without removing anything the policy needs.
whyWrong.B: Reuse only helps genuinely static content; forcing per-user data into the cache breaks freshness and risks serving one user's entitlements to another.
whyWrong.D: A safe-session check narrows but does not remove the risk, and still ties cache correctness to per-user state the caching layer was never meant to key on.

lessonKey: caching change content data find own per prefix reducing reject s savings static user

stem: A runbook requires alerts to fire on rate and segment drift, not individual events. The current setup pages on-call for every failed tool call across a system handling thousands of requests hourly. Which change complies with the runbook?

opts.t: Raise the per-event page threshold from one failure to fifty consecutive failures before paging.
Disable real-time paging and review a weekly aggregate error-count dashboard instead.
Replace per-event paging with alerts on error rate and per-segment rate thresholds, plus leading indicators such as escalation rate.
Add per-segment accuracy breakdowns to the existing quality dashboard for weekly review.

whyRight: The runbook forbids per-event alerts; alerting on error rate and per-segment rate thresholds, together with leading indicators like escalation rate, surfaces the same drift the current per-event paging catches, without generating a page for every isolated failure.

whyWrong.A: Raising the failure count before paging still alerts on individual events at a higher threshold; it never switches the mechanism to the rate and segment thresholds the runbook actually requires.
whyWrong.B: Disabling real-time paging removes detection entirely between weekly reviews; the runbook calls for rate-based alerting, not the absence of any alert until the next scheduled check.
whyWrong.D: Per-segment dashboard breakdowns fix aggregate reporting, a genuinely different problem; they do not change how or when the on-call engineer is paged for a single failed call.

t1Clause: the current setup pages on-call for every failed tool call

stem: A new document-ingestion pipeline goes live; audits then find some responses leak another policyholder's identifier, though the model and prompt are unchanged. A regulator requires outputs never expose another policyholder's identifier. How should the team classify and enforce this?

opts.t: Classify it as a safety issue only and add identifier-leak wording to the model-graded quality rubric.
Log every response containing a policyholder identifier and review the log weekly for repeat leaks.
Add a system-prompt instruction reminding the model never to reveal another policyholder's identifier.
Treat it as both a safety and security requirement, enforced by a deterministic identifier scan on every output.

whyRight: An identifier leak is both a safety failure, since it is emitted content, and a security failure, since some scoping or filtering gap let it through; a deterministic scan is the exact-match instrument the corpus assigns to a requirement enforceable as a hard zero.

whyWrong.A: Safety-only classification fits harm that lives purely in wording, such as discriminatory language; an identifier is exact, checkable content, and its leak also reflects a permission or scoping failure.
whyWrong.B: Logging leaks for weekly review only detects exposure after it already reached the user; the requirement needs a deterministic check that blocks the identifier before the response goes out.
whyWrong.C: A prompt reminder is advisory and fails at the tail; the corpus treats identifier exposure as a hard-zero property enforceable by a deterministic pattern check, not a model instruction.

t1Clause: some responses leak another policyholder's identifier
lessonKey: both check control deterministic enforcing pii

stem: A team proposes a new model grader to score tone and helpfulness, and the compliance team will approve reducing human review once the grader reports a passing average. What must happen before any score from this new grader is trusted?

opts.t: Hand-label 20 to 50 cases, run the grader on them, and compute agreement with the human labels before deciding.
Increase the number of graded outputs from 100 to 1,000 for a more statistically reliable average.
Set a fixed passing bar now and begin reporting the grader's average starting next quarter.
Use the grader now, but label every resulting score as degraded until further notice.

whyRight: A model grader is itself an unvalidated instrument until its agreement with human labels is known; hand-labeling a working sample and computing that agreement is the step the corpus requires before any score, including one gating a reduction in human review, is trusted.

whyWrong.B: More graded outputs tighten the confidence interval around whatever the grader already reports; it does nothing to establish whether the grader's judgments agree with a human's in the first place.
whyWrong.C: Setting a bar and reporting a number treats an uncalibrated grader's output as meaningful; the scale itself is undefined until agreement with human labels has actually been measured.
whyWrong.D: Marking scores degraded is the right move only when no other grader is available; here a fresh grader is being proposed and validating it against human labels is still possible.

t1Clause: a team proposes a new model grader (implying it is not stated as the only grader available)
lessonKey: 20 50 agreement cases compute decide grader hand label run then

stem: A prompt change shipped to 100% of traffic two weeks ago with no control arm. Quality metrics improved three points, but traffic mix and a model-provider update also shifted in that window. What can the team conclude?

opts.t: State that no clean comparison exists; the before/after result is confounded by everything else that shifted in the same window.
Conclude the prompt change alone caused the improvement, since it was the only intentional change made.
Build a causal attribution model over the shifted variables to isolate the prompt change's individual contribution.
Run the regression set first, then a controlled A/B, before crediting the prompt change with the improvement.

whyRight: Without a held-out control arm, the historical improvement is confounded by everything else that shifted in the same window; the corpus requires stating that no clean comparison exists rather than crediting the already-shipped change with the gain.

whyWrong.B: The stem states traffic mix and a model-provider update also shifted in the same window, directly ruling out treating the prompt edit as the improvement's sole cause.
whyWrong.C: A causal model fit after the fact does not recover the missing control arm; it manufactures rigor around already-confounded data instead of admitting the comparison was never clean.
whyWrong.D: Regression-then-A/B is the right order before a change ships; this change already reached 100% of traffic two weeks ago, so the step cannot retroactively unconfound a historical result.

t1Clause: the change already shipped to 100% of traffic two weeks ago with no control arm

stem: An assistant reviewing thousand-page compliance contracts answers correctly on short excerpts but misses facts stated in the middle of long documents, though the documents fit well within the context window's token limit. Which change most directly addresses this pattern?

opts.t: Move to a higher-capability model, since the current model cannot reliably track facts across long documents.
Increase the context window's maximum token limit to accommodate longer documents.
Add an explicit instruction telling the model to read the entire document carefully before answering.
Restructure how content is positioned in context, moving critical facts away from the middle of long documents.

whyRight: Facts lost mid-document while short excerpts succeed, and the window is not exceeded, is the corpus's context-structure signature; the fix repositions critical content, since model capability, window size, and instruction wording are not the layer at fault here.

whyWrong.A: The model is not implicated: accuracy depends on where a fact sits in the document, matching the context-structure signature, not the broad reasoning failure that names a genuine mismatch.
whyWrong.B: The documents already fit within the current window; enlarging a limit that is not exceeded does not change how position bias buries facts in the middle.
whyWrong.C: More prose instruction is the fix the corpus already rules out for format inconsistency despite explicit instructions; it does not change how the model weights content by position.

t1Clause: though the documents fit well within the context window's token limit
